title: Three places to uncover Boise's haunted history this fall
excerpt: If you are looking to encounter your first paranormal experience these three locations uncovers Boise’s haunted history
content:
As the leaves turn crisp, the wind begins to howl and nights grow longer, Boise’s ghosts come out to play — or at least, their haunting stories do. 

Between the whispers that are said to echo empty cell blocks, the creaking walls that harbor a part of Boise’s most gruesome history and a university building that is rumored to be inhabited by a ghost or two, the City of Trees has its fair share of spooky secrets. 

Whether you are looking to encounter your first paranormal experience or uncover the dark secrets behind Boise’s darkest history, these three locations offer a glimpse into the city’s haunted lore this fall.

Old Idaho State Penitentiary

With crumbling cell blocks and rumors of unexplained whispers, the Old Idaho State Penitentiary has become Boise’s most popular destination for paranormal enthusiasts.

“Boise doesn’t have a whole lot of other things like this,” said Jacey Brain, business operations specialist and visitor services coordinator for the Idaho State Historical Society. “Because people have developed such an interest in those things, true crime and haunted places, we built several of our programs around that interest.”

For the past 15 years, the penitentiary hosts paranormal investigations through Big River Paranormal, a regional paranormal investigative group. These investigations are open to the public several times throughout the year, but tickets sell out quickly. 

If you are lucky enough to snatch yourself a spot, visitors have reported feeling touches, hearing whispers and one investigator even recalls feeling someone run their hands through her hair and whisper, “Ohh, pretty,” according to Brain. 

The solitary confinement cell blocks are reported as the site’s most unsettling locations. Having harbored some of Idaho’s worst criminals, the cells carry a history that continues to draw visitors who are hoping to catch a glimpse of something unexplainable. 

Among the list of Idaho’s worst monsters, convicted murderer Raymond Snowden spent some time within solitary confinement before his attempted 1957 execution. Snowden is said to continue roaming the torn walls of his maximum security cell. 

“He is a Boise dark legend. People go to death row and that’s who they read about,” said Brain. “It is a dark chapter in Boise history.”

The Old Idaho State Penitentiary opens its doors year-round for those that are brave enough to step inside. 

Haunted Murder (“Chop-chop”) House on Linden Street

Behind what started as an innocent family home lies a dark history straight out of a horror film. Known as the “Chop-chop House,” the infamous property is  rumored to foster paranormal activity following the gruesome murder of Idahoan Preston Murr in 1987. 

The incident  fueled immense fascination among the locals intrigued by the paranormal. Numerous reports of chilling climate and eerie sensations follow those who go near the home. Although property owner, James Howell, denies many paranormal rumors surrounding  the house, previous tenants have reported eerie encounters, including unexplained shadows and unsettling noises.  

James Swain, the home’s caretaker, expressed that although he hasn’t personally experienced any paranormal activity while residing on the property, he witnessed some chilling reports. 

“One lady came by with her husband,” said Swain. “They showed me an old picture where there was a shadow up (in the upstairs window) 

While there isn’t much to prove the existence of Preston Murr’s spirit residing in the home, Swain understands why places like the Linden Street Murder house excite paranormal enthusiasts.

When asked why some became so fascinated with the home, Swain explains, “So they can believe, you know? That there is an afterlife.” 

The property remains closed to the public, but you can still drive by 805 W Linden Street if you dare.

Boise State’s “Haunted” Communication Building

For many Boise State students, the Communication Building has become a familiar place to work and study. However, rumor has it that this building might be home to something other worldly.

Before its conversion into the Communication Building, the building previously served as the university’s Student Union Building. A young woman named Dinah, who allegedly died within the building’s walls after being rejected by a date at a dance, and some say she still roams the halls. 

Mackenzie White, an equipment room employee and senior, claims to have her own paranormal encounter after hours.

While working late one night, White heard what sounded like footsteps followed by a series of knocks coming from the upstairs computer lab. The catch? That section of the building is closed off. 

“It knocked a few times, and then it just stopped,” said White. “It was 11 p.m. and I knew it was time to go home after that.”

Although there is no official documentation from the university’s archives that proves Dinah’s existence, White believes that the urban legend has persisted all these years because of its deep connection to campus life. Media students spend early mornings and late nights within the building, making paranormal reports hit closer to home.

“We’re always here,” White said. “We are always hearing stories about other people [‘s experiences], and some of us have experienced things ourselves.”

What some may view as another ordinary university building, for the students that work after hours, a knock in the night can send shivers down even the bravest Bronco’s spine

Whether it’s a low whisper behind a prison wall, a shadowy figure looking at you from the window frame or a knock echoing through an empty hall, the scariest part isn’t what we are able to see, but what we can’t explain.
